claim: Recent theories propose that schizophrenia/schizotypy and autistic spectrum disorder are related to impairments in Bayesian inference.
source: Recent theories propose that schizophrenia/schizotypy and autistic spectrum disorder are related to impairments in Bayesian inference that is, how the brain integrates sensory information (likelihoods) with prior knowledge.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to theoretical frameworks in the literature.

claim: Existing accounts fail to clarify how proposed theories differ in accounts of ASD vs. schizophrenia.
source: However existing accounts fail to clarify: (i) how proposed theories differ in accounts of ASD vs. schizophrenia and (ii) whether the impairments result from weaker priors or enhanced likelihoods.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, based on the authors' review.

claim: Existing accounts fail to clarify whether the impairments result from weaker priors or enhanced likelihoods.
source: However existing accounts fail to clarify: (i) how proposed theories differ in accounts of ASD vs. schizophrenia and (ii) whether the impairments result from weaker priors or enhanced likelihoods.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, based on the authors' review.

claim: 91 healthy participants were scored for autistic and schizotypal traits.
source: Here, we directly address these issues by characterizing how 91 healthy participants, scored for autistic and schizotypal traits, implicitly learned and combined priors with sensory information.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and participant sample.

claim: The acquisition of the priors was found to be intact along both traits spectra.
source: The acquisition of the priors was found to be intact along both traits spectra.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Autistic traits were associated with more veridical perception.
source: However, autistic traits were associated with more veridical perception and weaker influence of expectations.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Autistic traits were associated with weaker influence of expectations.
source: However, autistic traits were associated with more veridical perception and weaker influence of expectations.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Bayesian modeling revealed that the effects of autistic traits were due to more precise sensory representations, not to weaker prior expectations.
source: Bayesian modeling revealed that this was due, not to weaker prior expectations, but to more precise sensory representations.
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling of the experimental data.

claim: Bayesian inference has come to be regarded as a general principle of brain function.
source: In recent years Bayesian inference has come to be regarded as a general principle of brain function that underlies not only perception and motor execution, but hierarchically extends all the way to higher cognitive phenomena, such as belief formation and social cognition.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field, based on established scientific consensus.

claim: Impairments of Bayesian inference have been proposed to underlie deficits observed in schizophrenia.
source: Impairments of Bayesian inference have been proposed to underlie deficits observed in mental illness, particularly schizophrenia (Fletcher and Frith, 2009; Corlett et al., 2009; Adams et al., 2013; Hemsley and Garety, 1986; Friston, 2005; Stephan et al., 2006) and autistic spectrum disorder (ASD) (Pellicano and Burr, 2012a; Van de Cruys et al., 2014; Lawson et al., 2014; Palmer et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Impairments of Bayesian inference have been proposed to underlie deficits observed in autistic spectrum disorder (ASD).
source: Impairments of Bayesian inference have been proposed to underlie deficits observed in mental illness, particularly schizophrenia (Fletcher and Frith, 2009; Corlett et al., 2009; Adams et al., 2013; Hemsley and Garety, 1986; Friston, 2005; Stephan et al., 2006) and autistic spectrum disorder (ASD) (Pellicano and Burr, 2012a; Van de Cruys et al., 2014; Lawson et al., 2014; Palmer et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: The general hypothesis for both schizophrenia and ASD is that the weight ascribed to sensory evidence and prior expectations is imbalanced.
source: The general hypothesis for both disorders is that the weight, also called 'precision', ascribed to sensory evidence and prior expectations is imbalanced, resulting in sensory evidence having relatively too much influence on perception.
evidence: This is a statement about theoretical frameworks in the literature.

claim: In schizophrenia, overweighting of sensory information could explain the decreased susceptibility to perceptual illusions.
source: In schizophrenia, overweighting of sensory information could explain the decreased susceptibility to perceptual illusions (Notredame et al., 2014), as well as the peculiar tendency to jump to conclusions (Speechley et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by citations.

claim: In schizophrenia, overweighting of sensory information could explain the tendency to jump to conclusions.
source: In schizophrenia, overweighting of sensory information could explain the decreased susceptibility to perceptual illusions (Notredame et al., 2014), as well as the peculiar tendency to jump to conclusions (Speechley et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by citations.

claim: Systematically weakened low-level prior expectations in schizophrenia might lead to forming compensatory strong and idiosyncratic high-level priors (beliefs).
source: Moreover, the systematically weakened low-level prior expectations might lead to forming compensatory strong and idiosyncratic high-level priors (beliefs), which would explain the emergence and persistence of delusions as well as reoccurring hallucinations (Fletcher and Frith, 2009; Corlett et al., 2009; Adams et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by citations.

claim: In ASD, the relatively stronger influence of sensory information could explain hypersensitivity to sensory stimuli.
source: In ASD, the relatively stronger influence of sensory information could explain hypersensitivity to sensory stimuli and extreme attention to details.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about ASD.

claim: In ASD, the relatively stronger influence of sensory information could explain extreme attention to details.
source: In ASD, the relatively stronger influence of sensory information could explain hypersensitivity to sensory stimuli and extreme attention to details.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about ASD.

claim: The weaker influence of prior expectations in ASD would result in more variability in sensory experiences.
source: The weaker influence of prior expectations would also result in more variability in sensory experiences.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about ASD.

claim: The desire for sameness and rigid behaviors in ASD could be understood as an attempt to introduce more predictability in one's environment.
source: The desire for sameness and rigid behaviors could then be understood as an attempt to introduce more predictability in one's environment (Pellicano and Burr, 2012a).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: All theories agree that the relative influence of prior expectations is weaker in ASD.
source: While all theories agree that the relative influence of prior expectations is weaker in ASD, the primary source of this imbalance is debated: does it arise from increased sensory precision (i.e. sharper likelihood) or from reduced precision of prior expectations?
evidence: This is a statement about the consensus and debate in the literature.

claim: The primary source of the imbalance in ASD is debated: does it arise from increased sensory precision or from reduced precision of prior expectations.
source: While all theories agree that the relative influence of prior expectations is weaker in ASD, the primary source of this imbalance is debated: does it arise from increased sensory precision (i.e. sharper likelihood) or from reduced precision of prior expectations? (Brock, 2012; Pellicano and Burr, 2012b; van Boxtel and Lu, 2013) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the debate in the literature, illustrated by Figure 1.

claim: Some authors argue for attenuated priors in ASD.
source: Some authors argue for attenuated priors (Pellicano and Burr, 2012a; Pellicano and Burr, 2012b), while others argue for increased sensory precision (Lawson et al., 2014; Palmer et al., 2017; Brock, 2012; Van de Cruys et al., 2013) but conclusive experimental evidence is lacking.
evidence: This is a statement about different theoretical positions in the literature.

claim: Some authors argue for increased sensory precision in ASD.
source: Some authors argue for attenuated priors (Pellicano and Burr, 2012a; Pellicano and Burr, 2012b), while others argue for increased sensory precision (Lawson et al., 2014; Palmer et al., 2017; Brock, 2012; Van de Cruys et al., 2013) but conclusive experimental evidence is lacking.
evidence: This is a statement about different theoretical positions in the literature.

claim: Conclusive experimental evidence is lacking for whether ASD involves attenuated priors or increased sensory precision.
source: Some authors argue for attenuated priors (Pellicano and Burr, 2012a; Pellicano and Burr, 2012b), while others argue for increased sensory precision (Lawson et al., 2014; Palmer et al., 2017; Brock, 2012; Van de Cruys et al., 2013) but conclusive experimental evidence is lacking.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: The enhanced sensory precision hypothesis predicts reduced perceptual variability in ASD.
source: However, these alternatives differ in their predictions for perceptual variability, which is determined by the posterior width: the enhanced sensory precision hypothesis should lead to reduced variability while the attenuated prior hypothesis should lead to increased variability.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The attenuated prior hypothesis predicts increased perceptual variability in ASD.
source: However, these alternatives differ in their predictions for perceptual variability, which is determined by the posterior width: the enhanced sensory precision hypothesis should lead to reduced variability while the attenuated prior hypothesis should lead to increased variability.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The experimental paradigm can distinguish between the enhanced sensory precision hypothesis and the attenuated prior hypothesis by measuring both bias and variability.
source: By measuring both bias and variability, our experimental paradigm can distinguish between these two hypotheses.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design capabilities.

claim: A number of studies have aimed at testing Bayesian theories in a clinical population or by studying individual differences in the general population.
source: A number of studies have aimed at testing Bayesian theories, either in a clinical population, or by studying individual differences in the general population (Powell et al., 2016; Skewes et al., 2015; Teufel et al., 2015; Schmack et al., 2013) under the hypothesis of a continuum between autistic/schizotypal traits and ASD/schizophrenia (Nelson et al., 2013; van Os et al., 2009; Constantino and Todd, 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about the literature, supported by citations.

claim: There is a hypothesis of a continuum between autistic/schizotypal traits and ASD/schizophrenia.
source: A number of studies have aimed at testing Bayesian theories, either in a clinical population, or by studying individual differences in the general population (Powell et al., 2016; Skewes et al., 2015; Teufel et al., 2015; Schmack et al., 2013) under the hypothesis of a continuum between autistic/schizotypal traits and ASD/schizophrenia (Nelson et al., 2013; van Os et al., 2009; Constantino and Todd, 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about a theoretical hypothesis, supported by citations.

claim: Attenuated slow-speed priors were reported in a motion perception task in individuals with ASD traits.
source: Attenuated slow-speed priors were reported in a motion perception task in individuals with ASD traits (Powell et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: Autistic children showed attenuated central tendency prior in temporal interval reproduction.
source: Autistic children also showed attenuated central tendency prior in temporal interval reproduction (Karaminis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: Attenuated priors were reported in perceptual tasks that incorporate probabilistic reasoning.
source: Attenuated priors were also reported in perceptual tasks that incorporate probabilistic reasoning (Skewes et al., 2015; Skewes and Gebauer, 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from cited studies.

claim: The direction of gaze priors were found to be intact in individuals with high autistic traits.
source: However, the direction of gaze priors (Pell et al., 2016) and the light-from-above priors (Croydon et al., 2017) were found to be intact.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: The light-from-above priors were found to be intact in individuals with high autistic traits.
source: However, the direction of gaze priors (Pell et al., 2016) and the light-from-above priors (Croydon et al., 2017) were found to be intact.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: Autistic children demonstrated intact ability to update their priors in a volatile environment in a decision-making task.
source: Autistic children also demonstrated intact ability to update their priors in a volatile environment in a decision-making task (Manning et al., 2017) but a follow-up study in ASD adults showed that they overestimate volatility in a changing environment (Lawson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: ASD adults overestimate volatility in a changing environment.
source: Autistic children also demonstrated intact ability to update their priors in a volatile environment in a decision-making task (Manning et al., 2017) but a follow-up study in ASD adults showed that they overestimate volatility in a changing environment (Lawson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: Teufel et al. (2015) reported increased influence of prior expectations when disambiguating two-tone images in schizophrenia/schizotypal traits.
source: In schizophrenia/schizotypal traits, Teufel et al. (2015) reported increased influence of prior expectations when disambiguating two-tone images, while Schmack et al. (2015, 2017) reported weakened influence of stabilizing predictions when observing a bistable rotating sphere.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: Schmack et al. (2015, 2017) reported weakened influence of stabilizing predictions when observing a bistable rotating sphere in schizophrenia/schizotypal traits.
source: In schizophrenia/schizotypal traits, Teufel et al. (2015) reported increased influence of prior expectations when disambiguating two-tone images, while Schmack et al. (2015, 2017) reported weakened influence of stabilizing predictions when observing a bistable rotating sphere.
evidence: This is a finding from cited studies.

claim: The existing findings on Bayesian inference in ASD and schizophrenia are mixed.
source: Overall, the existing findings are not only mixed, but also employ very different paradigms, which makes their direct comparison difficult.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: Existing studies employ very different paradigms, which makes their direct comparison difficult.
source: Overall, the existing findings are not only mixed, but also employ very different paradigms, which makes their direct comparison difficult.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: A critical limitation of most studies is the lack of formal computational models that can test whether behavioral differences originate from different priors or from different likelihoods.
source: Further, a critical limitation of most studies (except for Karaminis et al., 2016) is the lack of formal computational models that can test whether behavioral differences originate from different priors or from different likelihoods.
evidence: This is a statement about methodological limitations in the literature.

claim: There is no previous work investigating both autistic and schizotypal traits within the same experimental paradigm.
source: Moreover, to our knowledge, despite the similarity of the Bayesian theories proposed for ASD and schizophrenia, there is no previous work investigating both autistic and schizotypal traits within the same experimental paradigm so as to test their differences.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: Chalk et al. (2010) found that healthy participants rapidly and implicitly develop prior expectations for the most frequently presented motion directions in a statistical learning task.
source: Chalk et al. (2010) found that in this task healthy participants rapidly and implicitly develop prior expectations for the most frequently presented motion directions.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: Prior expectations alter perception of motion on low contrast trials resulting in attractive estimation biases towards the most frequent directions.
source: This in turn alters their perception of motion on low contrast trials resulting in attractive estimation biases towards the most frequent directions.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study (Chalk et al., 2010).

claim: Prior expectations lead to reduced estimation variability for the most frequently presented directions.
source: In addition, prior expectations lead to reduced estimation variability and reaction times, as well as increased detection performance for the most frequently presented directions.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study (Chalk et al., 2010).

claim: Prior expectations lead to reduced reaction times for the most frequently presented directions.
source: In addition, prior expectations lead to reduced estimation variability and reaction times, as well as increased detection performance for the most frequently presented directions.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study (Chalk et al., 2010).

claim: Prior expectations lead to increased detection performance for the most frequently presented directions.
source: In addition, prior expectations lead to reduced estimation variability and reaction times, as well as increased detection performance for the most frequently presented directions.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study (Chalk et al., 2010).

claim: When no stimulus is presented, the acquired expectations sometimes lead to false alarms (hallucinations), mostly in the most frequent directions.
source: When no stimulus is presented, the acquired expectations sometimes lead to false alarms (hallucinations), again, mostly in the most frequent directions.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study (Chalk et al., 2010).

claim: Biases in the Chalk et al. (2010) task were well described using a Bayesian model.
source: Importantly, such biases were well described using a Bayesian model, where participants acquired a perceptual prior for the visual stimulus that is combined with sensory information and influences their perception.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study (Chalk et al., 2010).

claim: The paradigm is well suited to quantitatively model variations in likelihoods and priors in individuals with ASD or schizotypal traits.
source: As such, this paradigm is well suited to quantitatively model variations in likelihoods and priors in individuals with ASD or schizotypal traits.
evidence: This is a statement about the suitability of the experimental paradigm.

claim: Eight participants failed to perform the task satisfactorily and were excluded from the analysis.
source: Eight participants failed to perform the task satisfactorily and were excluded from the analysis (see Materials and methods), leaving 83 participants in the study (41 women and 42 men, age range: 18–69; mean: 25.7).
evidence: This is a description of the data exclusion criteria and final sample.

claim: 83 participants were included in the study (41 women and 42 men, age range: 18–69; mean: 25.7).
source: Eight participants failed to perform the task satisfactorily and were excluded from the analysis (see Materials and methods), leaving 83 participants in the study (41 women and 42 men, age range: 18–69; mean: 25.7).

claim: The first 170 trials were discarded because that is how long it took for the 2/1 and 4/1 staircases contrast levels to converge.
source: We discarded the first 170 trials as that is how long it took for the 2/1 and 4/1 staircases contrast levels to converge (Appendix 1—figure 2) and for prior effects to become significant (Appendix 1—figures 3, 4 and 5).

claim: The first 170 trials were discarded because that is how long it took for prior effects to become significant.
source: We discarded the first 170 trials as that is how long it took for the 2/1 and 4/1 staircases contrast levels to converge (Appendix 1—figure 2) and for prior effects to become significant (Appendix 1—figures 3, 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis procedure.

claim: On the group level people acquired priors that approximated the statistics of the task.
source: Replicating findings of Chalk et al. (2010), we found that on the group level people acquired priors that approximated the statistics of the task.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Attractive biases towards ±32° indicate that priors were acquired.
source: Such priors were indicated by: attractive biases towards ±32° (Figure 3a), less variability in estimations at ±32° (Figure 3b; standard deviation of estimations 11.9 ± 0.30° at ±32° versus 13.84 ± 2.38° over all other motion directions; signed rank test: p<0.001), shorter estimation reaction times at ±32° as compared to all other motion directions (Figure 3c; average reaction time was 201.87 ± 2.47 ms at ±32° versus 207.75 ± 2.60 ms over all other motion directions; signed rank test: p<0.001) and better detection at ±32° as compared to all other motion directions (Figure 3d; detected 75.57 ± 0.65% at±32° versus 66.70 ± 0.83% over all other motion directions; signed rank test: p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Standard deviation of estimations was 11.9 ± 0.30° at ±32° versus 13.84 ± 2.38° over all other motion directions (p<0.001).
source: less variability in estimations at ±32° (Figure 3b; standard deviation of estimations 11.9 ± 0.30° at ±32° versus 13.84 ± 2.38° over all other motion directions; signed rank test: p<0.001)
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Average reaction time was 201.87 ± 2.47 ms at ±32° versus 207.75 ± 2.60 ms over all other motion directions (p<0.001).
source: shorter estimation reaction times at ±32° as compared to all other motion directions (Figure 3c; average reaction time was 201.87 ± 2.47 ms at ±32° versus 207.75 ± 2.60 ms over all other motion directions; signed rank test: p<0.001)
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Detection was 75.57 ± 0.65% at ±32° versus 66.70 ± 0.83% over all other motion directions (p<0.001).
source: better detection at ±32° as compared to all other motion directions (Figure 3d; detected 75.57 ± 0.65% at±32° versus 66.70 ± 0.83% over all other motion directions; signed rank test: p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Participants sometimes reported seeing dots when no actual stimulus was presented (experienced hallucinations) but mostly so around ±32°.
source: We found that participants sometimes still reported seeing dots (experienced hallucinations) but mostly so around ±32° (Figure 3f, solid line).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The median of prel was significantly greater than 1 (median(prel)=1.6, p<0.001).
source: We found that the median of prel was significantly greater than 1 (median(prel)=1.6, p<0.001, signed rank test).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The estimation distribution when no dots were detected was significantly flatter (median(prel)=0, p<0.001).
source: Furthermore, the estimation distribution when no dots where detected (Figure 3f, dash-dot line) was found to be significantly flatter (median(prel)=0, p<0.001, signed rank test comparing with the median of prel for hallucinations), suggesting that the hallucinations were indeed of perceptual nature (rather than related to a response bias).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The hallucinations were of perceptual nature rather than related to a response bias.
source: Furthermore, the estimation distribution when no dots where detected (Figure 3f, dash-dot line) was found to be significantly flatter (median(prel)=0, p<0.001, signed rank test comparing with the median of prel for hallucinations), suggesting that the hallucinations were indeed of perceptual nature (rather than related to a response bias).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The AQ scores in the sample ranged from 6 to 41 with a mean (±SD) of 20.3 (±8.3).
source: The AQ scores in our sample ranged from 6 to 41 with a mean (±SD) of 20.3 (±8.3).
evidence: This is a description of the sample characteristics.

claim: The RISC scores ranged from 8 to 55 with a mean of 31.7 (±11.9).
source: The RISC scores ranged from 8 to 55 with a mean of 31.7 (±11.9), and the SPQ scores ranged from 4 to 59 with a mean of 26.4 (±13.8).

claim: The SPQ scores ranged from 4 to 59 with a mean of 26.4 (±13.8).
source: The RISC scores ranged from 8 to 55 with a mean of 31.7 (±11.9), and the SPQ scores ranged from 4 to 59 with a mean of 26.4 (±13.8).
evidence: This is a description of the sample characteristics.

claim: Autistic traits lead to less variability in estimations on low contrast trials (r = −0.327, p<0.001).
source: We found that on low contrast trials autistic traits lead to less variability in estimations (Figure 4b; mean standard deviation of estimations: r = −0.327, p<0.001), which remained significant after Bonferroni correction (p=0.002).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The correlation between autistic traits and less variability in estimations remained significant after Bonferroni correction (p=0.002).
source: We found that on low contrast trials autistic traits lead to less variability in estimations (Figure 4b; mean standard deviation of estimations: r = −0.327, p<0.001), which remained significant after Bonferroni correction (p=0.002).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was a negative relationship between autistic traits and estimation bias, which was trending according to robust regression (r = −0.175, p=0.053).
source: Moreover, there was a negative relationship between autistic traits and estimation bias, which was trending according to robust regression (Figure 4a; mean absolute estimation bias: r = −0.175, p=0.053) and significant according to Kendall's correlation (τb = −0.163, p=0.032), however, it did not survive Bonferroni correction (p=0.212).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The negative relationship between autistic traits and estimation bias was significant according to Kendall's correlation (τb = −0.163, p=0.032).
source: Moreover, there was a negative relationship between autistic traits and estimation bias, which was trending according to robust regression (Figure 4a; mean absolute estimation bias: r = −0.175, p=0.053) and significant according to Kendall's correlation (τb = −0.163, p=0.032), however, it did not survive Bonferroni correction (p=0.212).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The negative relationship between autistic traits and estimation bias did not survive Bonferroni correction (p=0.212).
source: Moreover, there was a negative relationship between autistic traits and estimation bias, which was trending according to robust regression (Figure 4a; mean absolute estimation bias: r = −0.175, p=0.053) and significant according to Kendall's correlation (τb = −0.163, p=0.032), however, it did not survive Bonferroni correction (p=0.212).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Observing less bias and less variability together suggests that the effects are driven by narrower likelihoods.
source: Thus, observing less bias and less variability together suggests that the effects are driven by narrower likelihoods.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Schizotypy traits (RISC and SPQ scores) did not show any effect on task performance at low contrast.
source: Schizotypy traits (RISC and SPQ scores) did not show any effect on task performance at low contrast as indicated by the absence of correlations with mean absolute estimation bias (RISC: r = 0.140, p=0.197; SPQ (N = 39): r = −0.160, p=0.204) and with mean estimation variability (RISC: r = 0.197, p=0.092; SPQ (N = 39): r = −0.229, p=0.171); see Appendix 1—figures 6, 7 and 8.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Autistic traits were associated with less hallucinations (r = −0.238, p=0.010).
source: We found that autistic traits were associated with less hallucinations (Figure 4c; r = −0.238, p=0.010), while schizotypal traits were found to have no effect on the number of hallucinations (RISC: r = 0.126, p=0.163; SPQ (N = 39): r = −0.010, p=0.959).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Schizotypal traits were found to have no effect on the number of hallucinations (RISC: r = 0.126, p=0.163; SPQ (N = 39): r = −0.010, p=0.959).

claim: Bayesian Kendall correlation analysis provided positive evidence that none of the traits had any effect on how hallucinations were distributed.
source: Bayesian Kendall correlation analysis on these measures provided positive evidence that none of the traits had any effect on how hallucinations were distributed, suggesting no differences in the acquired prior distributions (fraction of hallucinations within 8° of ±32°: AQ - τb = 0.003, BF01 = 7.24; RISC - τb = -0.050, BF01 = 3.73; SPQ - τb = 0.101, BF01 = 8.72; within 16° of ±32°: AQ - τb = -0.068, BF01 = 2.86; RISC - τb = -0.129, BF01 = 0.84; SPQ - τb = 0.018, BF01 = 5.45; within 24° of ±32°: AQ - τb = 0.057, BF01 = 11.67; RISC - τb = -0.078, BF01 = 2.40; SPQ - τb = 0.006, BF01 = 5.02).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The distribution of hallucinations suggests no differences in the acquired prior distributions across traits.
source: Bayesian Kendall correlation analysis on these measures provided positive evidence that none of the traits had any effect on how hallucinations were distributed, suggesting no differences in the acquired prior distributions (fraction of hallucinations within 8° of ±32°: AQ - τb = 0.003, BF01 = 7.24; RISC - τb = -0.050, BF01 = 3.73; SPQ - τb = 0.101, BF01 = 8.72; within 16° of ±32°: AQ - τb = -0.068, BF01 = 2.86; RISC - τb = -0.129, BF01 = 0.84; SPQ - τb = 0.018, BF01 = 5.45; within 24° of ±32°: AQ - τb = 0.057, BF01 = 11.67; RISC - τb = -0.078, BF01 = 2.40; SPQ - τb = 0.006, BF01 = 5.02).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The BAYES model had significantly smaller BIC values than the remaining models.
source: We found that the BAYES model had significantly smaller BIC values than the remaining models (see the p-values within Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a finding from the model comparison analysis, shown in Figure 6a.

claim: There was no correlation between AQ and the precision of the prior σexp (r = 0.018, p=0.962).
source: Correlational analysis of BAYES model parameters showed that there was no correlation between AQ and the precision of the prior σexp (Figure 7b; r = 0.018, p=0.962).
evidence: This is a finding from the model parameter analysis, shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Bayesian Kendall correlation provided positive evidence that autistic traits had no effect on the precision of the prior (τb = 0.001, BF01 = 6.99).
source: That autistic traits had no effect on the precision of the prior was confirmed by Bayesian Kendall correlation, which provided positive evidence (τb = 0.001, BF01 = 6.99).
evidence: This is a finding from the model parameter analysis.

claim: Autistic traits were strongly associated with less uncertainty in the sensory likelihood, σsens (r = −0.185, p=0.011).
source: Importantly, autistic traits were found to be strongly associated with less uncertainty in the sensory likelihood, σsens (Figure 7c; r = −0.185, p=0.011), which also remained significant after Bonferroni correction (p=0.044).
evidence: This is a finding from the model parameter analysis, shown in Figure 7c.

claim: The correlation between autistic traits and less uncertainty in the sensory likelihood remained significant after Bonferroni correction (p=0.044).
